utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There are a couple of administrative matters before we start. There's been an application made for protective measures. The name of the witness is confidential. The suggested pseudonym is K90. Mr. O'Sullivan, it would help the Chamber if someone could later today make submissions in response to this so that we can do something at the weekend, if necessary. I suggest right at the end of the day today because there's no trial in the afternoon, and if we run on for five minutes it won't matter. The other matter is the documents which were the subject of objection yesterday, and the Trial Chamber has a comment to make to supplement what was said yesterday about these. Two of the documents have already been admitted, and these are P1960 and P1427. There was some confusion over the numbers of the two referred to by Mr. Ivetic at the end, but ultimately I've noted these as P1249 and P1996, and if these are the accurate numbers then neither of these has already been admitted. So far as the rest are concerned, I draw the attention of parties, but particularly the Prosecution, to first of all the terms of the decision dealing with the motion to admit stand-alone documents. That decision was the 10th of October last year, and in particular paragraphs 37 and 39, which make it clear how the exercise should be approached. And it's surprising to us that greater use of this suggested approach has not been made so far. Parties will also remember that on the 14th of December various things were said in a similar context, and I think it worthwhile repeating what I said ultimately then, and this is referring to the motion that was dealt with on the 10th of October. The motion to which you've referred was a motion inviting us to admit material without really seeing how it would fit into the case, and we admitted what was obvious to us as relevant material and also authentic material. In making any further submissions for the admitting of documents standing alone, you should be directing the Trial Chamber's attention to the passages that are relevant to the case and to the question how they are relevant to the case. Now, it's for you in making that submission to judge in your own mind whether the whole of the document also needs to be admitted to enable a full understanding of the situation given to the Trial Chamber, but please bear in mind that we - I don't know whether it's been the practice in the past or not - but we are not prepared to accept large volumes of material that might later feature in an argument that has been put together. This case has been on the go for so long that parties ought to know what their case is and where documents fit into it, and we expect to be assisted in that way. Now, that's the best guidance I can give you. If you take the view that you throw material at us because it might be relevant in view of the heading, then you're making a big mistake and we will reject it, and we may as a result of that miss the nuggets that are in it. There was also a footnote on the -- one of the decisions which, again, it would be helpful to repeat. The Trial Chamber's notes the Prosecution's concern about the fact that many of the authors of the documents are unavailable to testify; however, should these documents be offered for admission during trial the witness need not necessarily be the author of the document in question. The witness need only be capable of testifying to the contents of the documents. We thought it useful to remind parties of these earlier comments. It may be that as we proceed with the evidence of this witness, we will have to address individual documents. So far as the one that arose yesterday was concerned, that was P1000 I think, there is on the face of it no reason at the moment why that should be admitted. The position may change.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, P1000 was Milosevic Exhibit 387, tab 37, and it relates to his testimony that was offered in this case. And for the purposes of helping you understand his testimony in that case, it relates to transcript page 15961 at line 6. I believe it has been our practice in the past when we offer transcripts that we offer the related exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Hannis, and it may be that that's the context at which you have to look at it, but so far as it arose yesterday it wouldn't have been admitted in these circumstances. I accept that we'll have to address later the ones that feature as exhibits in the Milosevic transcript. But it may be that submissions have to be made by the Defence on that before we decide how we're going to deal with them. It's one thing to let in the odd document here and there and a transcript for the sake of understanding; it's quite a number when there's quite a large volume of documents referred to as a witness. And we as the Trial Chamber don't really see the relevance of them. So we'll address that later. I think we can now return to the witness; can we have him, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. We're now ready to continue with your evidence. Mr. Hannis will continue. I remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning to speak the truth will continue to apply to your evidence all the way through it, no matter how long you're here. I don't intend to remind you of that again, but it's a normal to remind you at least on the first occasion you return to court. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Yesterday we had begun to talk about the MUP and some of the special units associated with it. You discuss this in your statement beginning with paragraph 28. In paragraph 29, you talk about the OPGs or the Operational Sweep Groups. And in paragraph 29, you mention that according to reports from the security organs, the OPGs had expelled people in Kosovo, Mitrovica, and you mentioned some other crimes. With regard to the OPGs, was your source of information anyone else other than the security organs of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the security organs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could at this moment go into private session to cover one matter in -- relating to paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we went into private session a couple times yesterday, and I think I know the reasons for at least one of them, but there's been no application by the OTP specifying why we need to go into private session and why certain testimony is not to be done in public. And I may even agree if a reason is stated, but I would -- not knowing the reason I find it very hard to take a position on the matter and I would have to, therefore, object on principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To explore this, do we need to be in private session -- I mean to explore whether we should go into private session do we also need to be in private session, Mr. Hannis, or can it be done without doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into private session to explore the basis for this; and before we proceed with the evidence, we will undoubtedly return to public session to make our position clear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Having reviewed the position, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that it is appropriate that the evidence that we are now dealing with should be heard in private session. It's a fairly short passage of evidence. We're also satisfied in relation to two later incidents -- instances of evidence that have been addressed while we've been in private session, that evidence in relation to them should be in private session, but we'll deal with them individually when we reach them. We'll now return to private session for the current evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, we're back in open session. In paragraph 31 of your statement, you mention that at the later 17 May meeting with Milosevic, which we'll talk about in more detail in a while, that you told them who their superior was. I want to be clear, do you mean at that meeting you advised Milosevic and the others who the superior or the commander was for these OPGs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right now, at the previous session, the name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, the name you mentioned in closed session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move on to paragraphs 32 through 36 of your statement, where you talk about the JSO or the Special Operations Unit. I understand that the JSO was under the RDB or the state security side of the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The correct name is the department of state security or the sector of state security. In the organisation of the MUP, there are two sectors; the sectors of state security and the sector of public security. The head of the state security sector in 1999 was Rade Markovic. Within the state security sector, there is a unit for special operations, JSO, that was established sometime in 1996, and the precursor of that unit were the so-called Red Berets. They also had other names such as Grey Wolves. The beginning of their establishment dates back to 1991, which we see from their emblem, on which 1999 [as interpreted] is indicated as the year of establishment. That unit, according to our knowledge, was made up mostly of men who had been in other theatres of war previously across Yugoslavia; primarily in Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I may, give a narrative of all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something in the transcript. Maybe it's a mistranslation. Yes, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Me, too. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On line 14, it says we see from their emblem on which 1999 is indicated as the year of establishment. Did you mean 1999? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm sorry I interrupted you. Did you want to add something about the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were recognisable by their good weapons, weapons that actually exceeds the quality needed by a special operations unit. They had, for instance, the MiG 124 helicopter that even the army didn't have. They had Hummer vehicles. They had all sort of special ordnance. They wore the latest NATO-style uniforms in green colour. And wherever they appeared, it was obvious to which unit they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosnia and Croatia. Were you aware that the Red Berets had engaged in action during the war in Croatia and Bosnia in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware that at least certain members of the Red Berets were alleged to have committed a number of crimes during those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is bordering on becoming a leading question, so I would have to object at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does look like a leading question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there certainly is plenty of public evidence that Red Berets have been alleged to be involved in crimes in Bosnia and Croatia. I'm just asking if he's aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're relying on the use of the word "alleged"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I think I don't see a problem with that, Mr. Ivetic. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not necessary. During the war in Bosnia, I was, objectively speaking, retired; however, through the mass media and some trials that had taken place and through communications with people from the service who were working then, I had knowledge that these units -- it was known that these units had been in Bosnia and that they were involved in some crimes. There was a trail of crimes behind them. Let me explain who the men making up the unit were. Some of them were drawn from Arkan's units, and one of them was the commander of the JSO, Ulemek, known as Legija. We had information that we were checking in 1991 concerning the 1st Corps of Arkan's men, and there were 19 men and 102 years of imprisonment between them. So with such a problematic unit, some of the men from that unit were admitted into the JSO, and one of them became commander of the JSO. So I don't think there's anything disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness has confined his answer to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, were you aware of allegations that the Red Berets engaged in any criminal activity during the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about the beginning of the training of those units that were called Red Berets, and many paramilitary groups that were active at the time held themselves out to be Red Berets. And their role began sometime in the spring 1991 in Golubic, and there were also active around Skabrnja and other places in Croatia. So I cannot really enumerate them by the place and say that this and that unit committed a crime in such and such a place, but I know that a video was shown in this courtroom that was made at the anniversary celebration of that unit in Kula. And it was shown there where they had been across Yugoslavia, and you can see that war had taken them almost everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware whether there were similar allegations about Arkan's Tigers having committed crimes in Bosnia and/or Croatia in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. But at 17, 13, I believe the witness said that their war path had taken them almost through the whole Croatia and not everywhere. Maybe this can be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, at the end of that last answer, you were referring to the video that was shown in the Milosevic trial. And you said "that they had been across," now what area were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the area of Croatia because the question was about the -- the involvement of those units in Croatia. So I mentioned specifically they had been across Croatia, not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For full clarity, are you aware of allegations that the Red Berets engaged in criminal activity during the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if -- I don't think we got to the answer of my last question. Were you aware that there were similar allegations about Arkan's Tigers having committed crimes in Bosnia and Croatia in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. It's this whole complex that was called Conglomerate, that was called paramilitary units and Red Berets. Arkan's group was not called the Red Berets at the time. They were called either Tigers or Arkan's men, and all who were around Arkan called themselves that way. They didn't call themselves Red Berets, but there was information about their activities around Prnjavor and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Milorad "Legija" Ulemek as a commander of the JSO in 1998 and 1999 and that he had been a Tiger with Arkan. Do you know where he is now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, when I just left Belgrade, he was still in detention on suspicion that he had organised the attempt at Prime Minister Djindjic's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And his boss in 1998 and 1999, who was his immediate superior in the MUP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that he was part of the state security sector, and the head of that sector was Rade Markovic. But the immediate direct communication with that unit and control of that unit, as far as I know, was in the hands of Franko Simatovic, and that is why those units were called on the ground Frenki's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're aware that Mr. Simatovic is currently under indictment and pending trial before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before Rade Markovic became head of that sector, who was the head of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when he was replaced, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're aware that he's also pending indictment -- under indictment and pending trial in this Tribunal, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where Rade Markovic is now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Markovic is in prison on suspicion that he had -- he was involved in the organisation of the attempt on Vuk Draskovic's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 34 and 35, you speak about an encounter that you and Colonel Antic had with the JSO in Trstenik. Where is Trstenik? Is it in Serbia or Kosovo? Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trstenik is located in central Serbia, halfway between the towns of Kraljevo and Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And remind us again who Colonel Antic was. What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Antic was head of the security division in the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why had you and Colonel Antic gone to that location?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to give you some background. After the meeting of the 17th of May, I and General Gajic were given the assignment by General Ojdanic to go to Kosovo and gather more detailed information about what was going on concerning crimes, looting, and the other problems that were reported at the meeting of the 17th of May. However, instead of going directly to Kosovo, we had to go to Krusevac because there had been a problem with the 7th Infantry Brigade, most of which had left its positions and with all of their equipment and weapons had returned to Krusevac. So we stayed in Krusevac until the 30th of May. As we were fulfilling our -- those duties in Krusevac, General Pavkovic contacted us, contacted the team, and I think Colonel Antic took the call, saying that there was a problem with the military department in Trstenik. The military department in Trstenik employed four reserve officers and some more personnel. When a group of armed JSO members burst in, they disarmed the two military policemen at the entrance. They turned upside down the whole archive, the files of the military department. They disarmed one officer, and they seriously injured one officer who resisted, and that officer had to be hospitalised. So I got orders to go to Trstenik and see what it was all about. When we arrived at the military department, I verified the situation that had been described to me before. And I also found out that the head of the security centre from Kraljevo had also been there and that I should meet with him, but he had gone already to the JSO unit, which was based in a nursery building. So with Colonel Antic and Colonel Gligorijevic, who was head of security in the military district of Nis, and Major Ganic, who was head of security at the military department of Krusevac, I went to that nursery building where we were told the unit was located. That entire part of town, that entire neighbourhood, was blocked by those men on Hummer vehicles. And when I introduced myself and said I was looking for the commander, five or six armed men with rifles in their hands accompanied us into the building. I knocked the door of the office where I was told the commander was, but somebody from inside yelled, "Yes?" And I said, entering, "I am General Vasiljevic," and he commanded me to sit down. I don't really know whether to go into all those details. But the seven men who were armed and who were behind us, they were standing against the wall behind me, and I had a heated exchange with that commander. He tried to fell he to the ground, and he didn't succeed; then his body-guard approached and tried to separate me from his commander. And when he did not succeed, the commander said, "Take that thing down there." And then he took the Hechler -- he took a Hechler and pointed it at my ribs. It was a critical situation. Colonel Gligorijevic tried to pull out his pistol, but those men behind him knocked the pistol out of his hand. The commander said twice, "Shoot," and this lieutenant said, "Please don't, it's my patron saint's day. Today I have blood up to my shoulders." And, eventually, the commander released me and said,"You are a dangerous man. Sit down." And when we sat down again, he asked Antic, "How many throats have you slit?" Antic said, "I don't know, a few." And he insisted, "How many?" And the answer was, "About ten." And the other said, "Give me your word of honour." The response was, "Word of honour." And then the man said, "You are a real man." And then this security man from Kraljevo came in, asked me what I was doing there, took me out of that room. And he told me that he didn't know who those men were either, but he had been told from Belgrade that he should extend them all his assistance and that Legija, who was their commander, would come later and clear up that whole situation. When we took off towards Krusevac --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. We have some other details about that in your statement and I want to follow up. You say you made a recording of that incident during the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took out a tape recorder that I had in my pocket during the conflict with my -- with their commander, so the whole conversation was recorded. They saw that this was recorded. That tape, as far as I know, was later on sent both to the President Milosevic and others, because Milosevic apparently didn't believe that something like that could have happened. Before I left Krusevac to go to Trstenik, I spoke with Frenki Simatovic on the phone. He told me that I shouldn't go to Trstenik because they would deal with the problems themselves. I told him that I had an order from General Pavkovic to go there. And he told me, "Don't go there. These people are mad men." I told him, "That's your problem if you have mad men on your composition," and that's how I interrupted that conversation and I left to Trstenik after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that in, I think, paragraph 36 that there were military court proceedings started, but they were never completed. So as far as you know, there were no successful prosecutions of anyone for that incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there weren't. When the military judiciary system was disbanded, the then-president of the military court, General Vukosav, told me that the case was still recorded as an attack by an unknown perpetrator against a state official, although everybody knew who that person was. It is still being considered that it was done by an unknown perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any way of linking this group and their activities to events in Kosovo, bearing in mind that what you're talking about just now is something that happened in central Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that that unit had arrived from Kosovo and that they were located in Trstenik because the airport is there in Trstenik, and I know that they had been in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I now want to move on to the issue of MUP reservist and volunteers. You mentioned in paragraph 37 of your statement that people with experience in Bosnia and Croatia and some with criminal backgrounds were integrated, sometimes as a group, in contravention of procedures. Now, you told us earlier about in the VJ in 1998/1999, there were prohibitions against incorporating volunteers as a unit. Do you know, were there -- was there any similar provision with regard to the MUP? Did they have any limitations on incorporating groups as volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer for the moment. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have heard no foundational evidence from this witness of having knowledge of being in the MUP, of having studied the MUP, had any training in the MUP, so asking him this line of questioning I believe is improper because it's basically asking him to speculate. He has to provide a foundation for the fact that this witness would have knowledge of the rules and procedures in the MUP and the types of units in the MUP and the "official" chain of command, which I've not heard yet. And I would, you know, have to keep objecting to this point throughout because essentially, again, we have a witness who is in the army and yesterday couldn't tell us who is the Supreme Command in the army and who is a member of that Supreme Command. I mean, it baffles the mind that he can talk about an organisation he was never a part of without giving details as to foundation which I think are required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was does he know, yes or no. If he the answer is no, then that's the end of it. If the answer is yes, he does know, then my next question is: How does he know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I'll allow you to ask these questions on the basis that you control the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, my question is, first of all, just a simple yes or no. Do you know whether or not there were any similar restrictions with regard to volunteers joining the MUP; that is, was there any limitation or any bar on groups joining the MUP, yes or no? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could answer by saying yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if you don't link my answer only to volunteers but also to the way the reserve ranks were replenished, not only volunteers. I know the criteria --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. You've answered yes. Mr. Hannis now has to explore something before we can go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you the next question then, General. How do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were rules pertaining to the times when I was in active service, providing for the criteria for selection of both the active and the reserve troops in the MUP. Some of the criteria, for example, are that these people are not under investigation, that they had not committed crimes, and so on and so forth. In any case, the reservists of the MUP for the most part were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop again. Did you have access yourself to these rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of the provisions that were in place for the people who applied to be members of the reserve composition of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because a similar situation existed in the army when it came to replenishing special units. The first category of recruits were soldiers who had been recruited in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, the question is very specific. How were you aware of the specific provisions that applied to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because those competition announcements were published. They were made public, they were public knowledge, and they were publicised in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand that answer. What do you mean these competition announcements were published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was a number of vacancies and when candidates were called to apply for education, either for the MUP or the military schools, then these vacancies were made public and they were accompanied by the criteria that people had to meet in order to apply. I did not have any specific criteria for the MUP, but these criteria were public knowledge and we knew what criteria people had to meet in order to become reserve policemen or members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Hannis, you must have access to documents that make the position clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not personally aware off the top of my head that we have those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not prepared to exclude this evidence, but we make it clear that it may have very difficult to give any significant weight to it, in view of the source and the vagueness so far of the witness's account of how he was aware of these general requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, just one question on your -- on your last answer. You're saying when there were vacancies available for people to go to the police school and join the MUP, those announcements also contained the prerequisites for someone to become a policeman, which included things like not having any prior criminal record. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any particular provision that said only individuals can apply, no groups permitted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such provision. The law regulated the ways reservists were recruited, both for the police and the army. That's why there were military territorial bodies, such as military districts and military departments in various municipalities. People could become MUP reservists if they met the criteria of age. They could not be older than 35. They should have had their military service completed in a certain unit. And what usually happened was that young men who served in the first category of the JNA, that is the military police, the sabotage units, were transferred from the MUP reserve forces [as interpreted] to the police reserve forces. And when their records were transferred from the military to the MUP, then they were assigned duties according to the MUP criteria. And people could not be recruited by anybody else but those who were officially in charge of that. And as for the groups, I don't know. There was this guy Boca of whom I will speak later, but in any case this procedure was well-regulated and there were no exceptions, either in the MUP or in the military. There were set rules as to how to replenish the reserve forces of both the MUP and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is a problem with the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At 27, 25, I believe the witness said were transferred from the VJ reserve force to the police reserve force, not the MUP reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That makes sense. The last part of the evidence isn't easy to -- of the answer isn't easy to follow, Mr. Hannis. Just a matter of interest for us, you had a witness here not so long ago, Mr. Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Ljubinko Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he not the sort of person who would have told us that with a proper foundation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure everything -- of everything that was discussed with him when he was here, but I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had some evidence I think about this, but not from him. Anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a man named Boca. I want to ask you about his group, and in paragraph 38 you talk about the Skorpions. In 1999, were you aware of the Skorpions as a unit that had participated in the conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you know about them? What information did you have about their activities in those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of many details with regard to the activities of this unit. I only know that they appeared as a paramilitary unit primarily in Slavonia and Baranja. We checked this unit and we received information on the 12th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you tell us that they were commanded by Boca, the nickname for Slobodan Medic, who was subordinate to Asaj, A-s-a-j, deputy commander, Zoran, Tutinac, Simovic who himself was subordinate to Zivko Trajkovic. Were you aware -- the information you received in May 1999 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"], what did that involve? What information was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 1998, I believe you referred to 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I meant 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, the deputy chief of the Pristina Corps for security came and wanted to deal with some problems, and Jugoslav Petrisic's group had arrived in Kosovo bypassing the procedure that involved the centre in Kocka. That was the problem. On that occasion, he told us the outlines of some events that had taken place in Kosovo. He told us that there were killings, looting, certain cases of rape, that they had investigated some of these cases. And more specifically at the moment he mentioned in addition to the information about the army, he mentioned the existence of Slobodan Medic's unit under the name of Skorpions. He told me more specifically that that unit in Podujevo sometime around the 28th of March or towards the end of March had committed a crime. They had stormed an Albanian house and they killed ten children and two elderly people who minded them at the time, and then they were moved to Prolom Banja. But that unit re-appeared in Kosovo again. This is the information we received on the 8th of May, and Djurovic arrived on the 7th of May. Based on this information, we asked from the counter-intelligence group, our counter-intelligence group in Novi Sad, to check the information and to check who Medic Slobodan was, what this unit, Skorpion was, and where they were at the moment. On the 12th of May, we receive an official note from the counter-intelligence group in Novi Sad, in which it was stated that Slobodan Medic and his unit had between 120 and 130 men who were gathered whenever the MUP had to send them out to perform an activity, that those men mostly had criminal pasts. They had been through the previous theatres of war in Croatia, and that the unit called Skorpions a few days before that, before the 12th of May, had returned from Kosovo but that two groups were again being prepared to go back to Kosovo. One group would be led by Dalibor Novakovic and the other group would be led by Zivan Sokolavacki or Zivan Cetnik and that Goran Hadzic was behind the rallying of these two groups. This is the information that we received about that group when we asked for information from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm going to talk about them again later on. At the beginning of your answer, you mentioned the deputy chief of the Pristina Corps for security. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer, you mentioned that the information you got back on the 12th of May indicated that some of these Skorpion members had criminal pasts and had been through previous theatres of war in Croatia. Did you know or did you have information that some of the Skorpions had also been engaged in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraphs 40 through 42 of your statement, you talk briefly about Arkan's Tigers and the presence of some of them in Kosovo, and I'll ask you more about that when we get to the 17th of May meeting. But it's not clear to me when you mention that Arkan had official identification of the Yugoslav MUP, that he carried a Serbian RDB identification card, as did members of his reserve, and that they wore MUP uniforms. Did -- would you classify them as a volunteer unit, or a MUP reserve, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that the question, particularly the way it's asked, is objectionable, particularly, because when I objected to foundation previously, the witness based his knowledge on documents that he said he saw in public newspapers relating to reserve and active. He did not give any foundation for any knowledge as to volunteers. So insofar as this question asks for volunteer units, I think that we at least have to have some foundation laid as to what knowledge and upon what that knowledge is based of volunteers within the MUP this witness has. Since even in the rather vague information previously, there was no mention of any -- any source for knowledge as to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw the question. I'm satisfied with what's in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, now I want to talk a little bit about paragraphs 43 through 46 of your statement, where you talk a little bit about the MUP chain of command. And in paragraph 45 of your statement you say: "Pursuant to the law, during a state of war, the MUP was engaged in combat activities -- when engaged in combat activities was to be subordinated to the VJ ..." And: "In 1999, the VJ sought to subordinate the MUP in line with that law. Ojdanic asked Milosevic to issue a subordination order." I would now like to show you Exhibit P1460 in connection with that. Now, this is dated the 19th of April, 1999, before you were re-activated, but I think I can ask you to comment on some aspects of this document.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the document be blown up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that. As a matter of fact, General, I have a hard copy I could have the usher hand you that it may be easier for you that way. General, you'll see in the upper left-hand corner this refers to the 3rd Army command, but immediately below that it refers to the Supreme Command Staff and has a document that has General Ojdanic's name below it. Is this -- does this refer to what you were talking about in connection with the VJ attempt to subordinate the MUP according to the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain what this is. The original appears to be some sort of telegraph or fax.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order that was sent by fax, and it had previously been encoded. It was sent to the command stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you next Exhibit 1459, and again I think I can hand you a hard copy with the help of the usher. Now, this document is dated the 25th of May, 1999. It appears to be from the command of the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff to the Chief of Staff in person, and that would have been General Ojdanic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the document comes from the commander of the 3rd Army at the time, General Pavkovic. It appears to be stamped and signed at the end.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing in dispute here. This is a document issued by the command of the 3rd Army sent to the Supreme Command Staff on the 25th of May, 1999, but I don't see the stamp of the Supreme Command Staff, which would prove that that document was indeed received by them, something that is visible an other documents. I can see here that it was sent, but I don't know whether it was received. I don't know whether there was something behind the last page. Maybe this was faxed through, and in that case there would be a stamp showing that the document was encoded. This is a document by the command of the 3rd Army. There is nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, it makes reference to your order of 18 April and it refers to a number 01/2024. Could you look back at Exhibit 1460 and tell us if that is the reference number on that exhibit from General Ojdanic. If you'll look under the heading Supreme Command Staff, there is a --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the basis of the order issued on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's time for our break, General. I would like you to read it because I want you to understand what the nature of the content is, and then I have some questions for you after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may he take the document and read it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just for the record, I believe that the General was asked whether he had seen this document before. He said he didn't and it is not clear on the transcript, and I'm talking about the -- okay, now this has been corrected. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it will be in order for him to have a hard copy before returning to give evidence, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And may we break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's time for us to break, Mr. Vasiljevic. If you'll go with the usher we'll resume in 20 minutes at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you have a chance to read that document during the recess?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I ask you some more questions about it, I want to refer for a moment to your statement paragraph 45. As we said before, you say Ojdanic had asked Milosevic to issue a subordination order; then you say the order was issued but was disregarded, and Pavkovic complained in writing to Ojdanic that subordination had not occurred as such -- as such an order from the MUP had not reached subordinate units. You go on then to say Ojdanic went to Milosevic, who told him that the MUP would be confronted about it, but in any event, he - meaning apparently Ojdanic - should not be too concerned as to the subordination order had not been issued as a result of problems in cooperation between the MUP and the army in Kosovo, but rather because of problems with the MUP in Montenegro. And you tell us you're aware of that exchange because General Ojdanic showed you his personal notes in the matter. Now, having read Exhibit 1459, can you tell us if this appears to be the written complaint that you told us Ojdanic had told you about receiving from Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, General Pavkovic, back on the 16th of May, 1999, when we were preparing for the meeting next day at Milosevic's office, presented some problems with the cooperation with the MUP, that MUP was accusing the army of not taking certain actions, and that the resubordination was not going well. So back on the 16th of May, as early as on the 16th of May, he reported to Ojdanic about that, and this is all concentrated in one document of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 46 of your statement, you mention that: "Although the MUP was not practically subordinated to the army in Kosovo, the two groups were coordinated." And you mention the Joint Command as filling this void and, in effecting de facto cooperation and coordination." And as a matter of fact, in Exhibit 1459, that's what General Pavkovic says in the very last sentence of that -- of that communication; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that takes us to topic of the Joint Command. In paragraphs 47 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not clear where that is, Mr. Hannis, in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Exhibit 1459, Your Honour, the last sentence where he suggests that the Supreme Command should take urgent measures to resubordinate the units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we may have 1460 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's 1460 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can I see 1459, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of the English when we get it up. Suggests annulling the order on resubordination and leaving command of the forces of the MUP in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior staff of the MUP through the Joint Command, as has so far been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. It's taking a little time for me to understand this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, now in paragraphs 47 to 49 you talk a bit about Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to that - and I don't object to that, I wanted to say something else - this witness was proposed in part as viva voce. As far as I can see, though, he's going paragraph through paragraph. So I'm wondering when Mr. Hannis intends to move on to viva voce testimony, and I think this might be the right moment. That's what would suit me at least. It doesn't mean that it's necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, viva voce simply means he's going to be asked some questions, and I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but through leading questions, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is an example of a witness who really is being asked to repeat most of what's in his statement anyway, and the statement's not -- it's a form of note for me, rather than in the end for shortening the evidence. But the -- as long as the Rules are not being broken, Mr. Fila, we can't stop it. If you feel that the statement is being used in an inappropriate way, then if you formulate such an objection we'll consider it. But what Mr. Hannis is doing is using the statement to focus the issues and then seeking expansion of the evidence about these various matters from the witness, and I agree with you that that very often leads to the witness repeating what is in the statement as well as adding a little more. But I don't think it breaks the rules, so let's continue. And if there is a particular matter concerning you, please raise it with me again. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, as I said, in paragraphs 47 through 49, you talk about Joint Command, and you tell us that you were told by Colonel Stojanovic that the Joint Command came into existence in 1998. You also make reference to that information in paragraph 84, that this apparently occurred after your attendance at a Joint Command meeting in June of 1999. Did Colonel Stojanovic tell you who had been on the Joint Command in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned it superficially. It was not a particular topic that we reviewed at the time, but it was mainly mentioned that those were representatives of the army with occasional involvement of General Samardzic, commander of the 3rd Army; most of the time, Colonel Pavkovic, commander of the Pristina Corps; and from the MUP, the generals, Obrad Stevanovic, Lukic, Djordjevic; and Mr. Matkovic from the police; Sainovic, and Minic -- and from the politicians, Sainovic, Minic, and Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about how often the Joint Command met in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that specifically, nor did I ask how many times they had met. He just told me that he did not participate in those meetings, he had not been invited, and he had an idea why, possibly because there were top people from Belgrade. It was a very high level, where he is a security officer in the corps was not invited to take part in the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that list that you've given, you say: "It was mainly mentioned that those were representatives of the army with occasional involvement of Samardzic ... most of the time Pavkovic." Now, these are the two -- the only two army personnel you mention. Were no other army names given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't tell me about it. It was on our way from this building where the security division to the building where the meeting was held; that's what he managed to tell me on the way. And as far as I remember, those names were referred to. And at the meeting, there were other people I will name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So for 1998, which is what we're discussing here, should we take it that General Ojdanic was not involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't mention General Ojdanic to me as participating in the work of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 83 of your statement, you mention that the colonel also told you that Stanisic was involved in work of the command for several months. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That relates to the organs from the State Security Sector. He stayed on for longer spells in Kosovo, Jovica Stanisic I mean. And from the State Security Sector in Pristina, there was also an employee of the RDB, the State Security Sector, Lukic -- in fact, not Lukic, rather Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to alert, I guess, Defence counsel and the Court that at the end of this witness's testimony, I propose to tender an exhibit P1468, which we describe -- this is a handwritten document which we describe as minutes of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in 1998. And we will ask you to take some of this witness's evidence about the participants into consideration in deciding whether or not it's authentic and reliable. And for further consideration of that issue, we ask you to actually take a look at the document itself and see who the participants are and the matters they are discussing, because we think in some regards the document is self-authenticating. Thank you. So the Defence will have an opportunity to cross-examine about that if they want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, next, General, I want to show you a document; this is P2166. And if I could have the assistance of the usher, I'll give you a hard copy of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I could have the hard copy of those other two documents back from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this is a document Mr. O'Sullivan has challenged the authenticity of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand that was his position, and I only have a couple of questions for this witness about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you should ask him to assist us to authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think this witness can help us very far in that direction, other than identifying the participants, but they're identified by name in the document itself as to who they are. As I said, this was a Defence exhibit in Milosevic and it appears to be authentic. It is signed by the note-taker, and the content itself, Your Honour, we would suggest is further self-authenticating, given the dates and the referral to other events. And we would ask you to take all those factors into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it does also have a seal and the witness has assisted us already with that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can ask him a question about that as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, do you see a seal on that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it was filed and recorded in the military office of the president of the republic as a military secret with a number, and the date of the 2nd November 1998, which means that it was introduced in some register of the military office. It was entered in it. And the second thing about the military secret stamp, the round stamp, I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us anything about the military office of the president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness said: I don't know which -- to whom this stamp belongs, and it's not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's close enough I think, so we can accept what you say. Mr. Hannis is trying to clarify something of that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did -- can you tell us anything about what the military office of the president was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the office of the president. That is made up of certain division dealing with military issues that are within the jurisdiction of the president of the republic, since he's supreme commander in wartime. And in peacetime, he controls and commands the army, and the military office takes minutes from the sessions of the Supreme Command. And this is a record from a meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff, and I don't know whether he attended meetings of that body. So the Military Council of Defence had this military office at its disposal, in fact the president of the republic has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see at the end of the document that it indicates the minutes were compiled by Lieutenant-General Susic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I know he was head of the military office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the president?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to the list of the persons attending, it appears that almost everyone is either a VJ member, a member of the MUP, or a government official, with one exception, Mr. Matkovic, who's listed as vice-president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, SPS. Do you know why a political party member would be involved in this inter-departmental staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he was involved in his capacity as a party member or a representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated, in an answer a short while ago about the Joint Command in 1998, that Mr. Matkovic was a participant, according to your source, Colonel Stojanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to another document at this point in time if you have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have any specific submission to make about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. We object to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document looks authentic, it refers to the attendance of personnel consistent with the earlier evidence of the witness about what he was told about who attended these meetings. We think there are sufficient indicia of authenticity to admit this document, and the real question is what weight, if any, ought to be given to it in due course, depending on developments in the evidence as we proceed. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would comment at this point, too, that I think there was some testimony from Mr. Tanic about a body that met in Belgrade that may refer to this, as well as I think there's some internal indicators of reliability within the document itself. Thank you. Now I want to show the witness Exhibit P2014; 2014, this is from the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the usher's help, General, I'll give you a hard copy, if I can have the other one back. Now, this was after you had been resubordinated -- or reinstated that the VJ, and this appears to be an order from General -- General Lazarevic. Have you had a chance to see that? Do you need some time to look through it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just look through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the general is looking at it, perhaps we could go to the last page of both the original and the B/C/S to see the signature and the seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen the document. I've looked through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, in your 30 years' experience in the VJ, did you have occasion to see orders directing combat, and can you tell us whether or not this order is generally consistent with that type of VJ order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a classical document, professionally drafted, precise, made by the command of the Pristina Corps. I don't see to whom it was submitted, that's the only thing, but at the top from this heading in the corner, it says "copy number 1." And it says that it was delivered to the command of the MUP, which means that there were more addressees, a number of commands it was delivered to; and then in this empty space, they would fill in to which command it was being submitted, and that's why perhaps at the bottom it is not indicated to whom the document was addressed, not all of them are indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take a little time to go through this, because you describe this as a classic military order, I believe. The order is to break-up and crush STS, or Siptar Terrorist Forces, in the Mount Drenica sector, and immediately below that there is a reference to a map. Is that typical for this type of order to have a map reference; and if so, why is that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's always an indication of a map and the section thereof, in order for the subordinate who received the document to be able to find the bearings and to be able to locate the sectors that are mentioned in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And item number 1 regards the enemy. Is this typical to start out by describing the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1 in any order always refers to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 2, General, refers to the tasks of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And is that typically what would be contained within this type of order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item 2 always contains the task of our forces, item 3 is always neighbouring forces, and item 4 is always a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if we could go to page 8 -- I'm sorry, page 5 of the English, item 5. Tasks of the unit. That would seem to be a standard entry in such an order as well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After item 4, which is the general decision by the commander on the use of the unit, items 5, 6, and so on specify concrete tasks for particular subordinated units. In this case, it is the corps with its reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that connection, item 5.1, in this particular order, lists for the 252nd Armoured Brigade with the PJP, Special Police Unit detachment, and JSO, special operations unit, shall attack along the Malisevo village, Klecka village, and the Lapusnik village, Javor village axis. Is that a typical description in a impart order action?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. First the general axis and then the particular axis of attack for the unit and its particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 8 of the English, item number 6 is entitled "Fire Support." Would that be a common heading for this type of order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that this order is not just customary, but it is of high quality. It was drafted professionally. Every order has also part referring to fire support, security support, intelligence support, combat security, psychological support. This is a very classical order, and it is similar to any other high-quality order that is drafted. And such orders are drafted based on the task that was received by the superior command, and this is task number 2, the task of the Pristina Corps. This was not defined by the commander of the Pristina Corps. He received it from his superior command, and it's up to him to break down the task and issue the task through his own order, where all the elements will be defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In some cases, would an order not contain all of those specific paragraphs, depending on whether they were appropriate or necessary? Would there always be a reference to morale and psychology, for example?-- Morale and psychological support?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these items are found in any order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you then a document number 1966, and I will give you a hard copy of this one if I can exchange with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I think you have seen this one before because you have referred to in your statement, but if you want to take a minute to double-check and be sure you are familiar with it. Let me know when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This one is apparently coming from the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. It's an order described as to route and destroy the Siptar forces in the Malo Kosovo area dated the 22nd March 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this contains at least some of the classical elements you described for us. If we go through them, we have the map, we have the enemy forces; and number 2 on page 2, we have Pristina Corps task; page 3, we have neighbours and a decision; page 4 of the English, we have tasks for the units; and those other elements that you described. However, this does not -- on the last page, it simply appears to have the typed name "Joint Command for KiM," Kosovo and Metohija, and there is no signature. Do you have that comment about that? This is different from a classical military order, which normally would have a commander's name and signature.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm. Here in the left top corner on page 1, there is a number under which this document was registered as having been received. If I'm not mistaken, the previous document showed the same three first digits, 44 -- 455. I can draw my conclusion based on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness should proceed because these three digits are really crucial. They indicate the Pristina Corps and that's why the Prosecutor has interrupted the witness, although I think that the witness should be allowed to proceed, Your Honour. Let me provide additional explanation. We have contested the authenticity. And if you're talking about the lack of signatures, lack of protocols, the documents that never existed and that have been obtained, God know's how, and the witness has never seen because he was not in service at the time, you should let him proceed because, Your Honour, you are listening to him as somebody who understands documents, as he were an expert witness not just a base witness. You can't take things for granted. You can't just see a document and take it for granted as being authentic, as being okay. The witness should be allowed to proceed and explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not trying to prevent him from proceeding. I was going to ask him if he could take the pen and point to us on the screen where he was talking about the three-digit number. And with the usher's assistance that's what I was going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can all see the three-digit number. Mr. Fila, this document, 1966 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"], was not one of those listed yesterday as challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you'll allow me to explain. This document has never been announced among the documents that would be used. If you look at the notification dated 11 January, this document is not contained therein; that is why we never measured this document. It was only subsequently, yesterday morning while I was explaining my objection, my learned friend came and told us that this document would be used. This document was not contained originally in the notification dated 11 January, hence the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document, ERN K052-0028 through 32 and the companion document right after are it, are referred to in paragraph 85 of the witness's statement and described with particularity, the first one bearing the number 455-56 and the other one containing 455-56/1; and then I did tell them yesterday or the evening before that I specifically intended to include it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we now know that the authenticity is challenged, so proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you were referring to the three-digit number in the upper left under Joint Command. Could you tell us about that. What is that number; first of all, the three-digit number and then the two-digit number that follows the dash.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three-digit number denotes the number in the protocol of the command that is in charge of that protocol and refers to a certain problem that is being treated to -- through some documents. This is the number under which the first document is filed; and if this is the first document that was created, then the number is 455-1. The second group of digits after the dash, this is the order of the documents that arrive and are registered under the numbers and the dates when they are received and when they are recorded in the protocol. As far as I could see on the previous order by the command of the Pristina Corps, the number 455 was the same, and I can drew a conclusion from that that this is the number that was entered in the protocol of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So do you associate the number 455 with the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only established a link between the document and the protocol of the Pristina Corps. This means that this problem was registered in the records of the Pristina Corps under this number, 455 dash something. And this particular order that I have before me now, this is the 56th document in the records that deals with problem number 455. And as far as I can conclude, problem number 455 is Siptar terrorism in Kosovo. If this is a document that was received on the 22nd of March, 1999, this means that this document, number 56, was preceded by 55 other documents relative to the use of the forces in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the document that we looked at first, the joint -- the Pristina Corps order for combat signed by General Lazarevic and sent to the MUP, we can go back to confirm, but my notes indicate that that number was 455-262. So that would have been the 262nd document relating to number 455, you say to that problem or topic; the 262nd document in the year 1999, because these sequential numbers start at the beginning of the year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this particular protocol or log-book was opened at the beginning of the year, but I'm not sure. Most commonly, if that problem continues in the following period, in order to avoid losing documents, then the same number is taken over to the next book, to the next protocol book, once the first book has been completed. This facilitates locating documents relative to a certain problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the one we looked at before, Exhibit P2014, and it had the number 455-262, was dated the 25th of May, 1999. So if I understand what you're saying correctly, during the approximate two month period between the 22nd of March, which we have on Exhibit P1966, and the 25th of May, which is on Exhibit P2014, it appears that there have been approximately 206 other documents generated during that two-month period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we leave this one, item number 13 on the last page of both the English and B/C/S, the last sentence before the signature line, which is just typed "Joint Command for KiM," it says: "The Joint Command for KiM shall command and direct all forces for combat operations for the Pristina area." Now, I want to show you P1967 and see if we can make a connection between those documents, and why don't you keep that hard copy and let me hand you now a hard copy of P1967. Now, General, this document is also dated the 22nd of March. It's entitled, "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," and its number is 455-56/1. Now, how would you interpret that numbering system? We've already got the 56th document related to this problem. What does 56/1 indicate?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that this document is directly connected to the previous one, which was 56, and that is why it is called "amendment to the decision." The previous document contained a decision of the command of the Pristina Corps -- I'm sorry, the Joint Command actually. So this is just a supplement, an amendment, to that previous order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And indeed that is the title of this document. It says: "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP in breaking up and destroying the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo," which is what document 1966 was, an order to route and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area. I note, however, that this one doesn't have the standard classical items of: One, the enemy; number two, the Pristina Corps tasks; and number three, adjacent or neighbouring parties. And why would that be, if you know or can tell us.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is just a supplement of the previous document. Now the order is complete. Now that you have the amendment, the order is complete. Whatever is contained in this order is relative to the previous order, i.e., the previous order should include the amendment in order to make it complete. This is just one problem. The first document was not signed. It was stamped by Joint Command or Joint Command was indicated, but here we can see the signature of the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
